# Mid-Market Support

`customer_support.model.mid_market_support` · model · parent `—`

> The awkward middle, and the awkwardness is structural rather than a sign of immaturity. There is a contract and there is an entitlement — real, machine-checkable, with a response target written in it — and nobody on either side has read it. It was chosen as a checkbox late in a short sales cycle by a buyer optimising for licence price, so the agent typically discovers what was promised at the moment it is about to be missed, and the customer discovers it when they are told something is not in their plan. That sentence — "that is not included in your tier" — is the most expensive one in the model, because it is a commercial conversation being conducted by someone who does not own the commercial relationship. . There is no support organisation on the other side and no procurement process. One admin owns the tool alongside four other jobs, and that person is the deployment's entire institutional memory: they know why the integration is configured the way it is and nobody else does. When they leave, ticket quality collapses in a way that looks like a product regression and is not, and the account gets quietly harder to serve for a year. . Escalation has no ladder to climb, so it goes sideways. It travels through the AE or the CSM into the commercial relationship and arrives as a forwarded email from our own colleague rather than as a request from the customer — which means the participant list on a mid-market escalation includes people whose incentive is to promise things support has not agreed to. . What an operator carries over wrongly from enterprise: assuming there is a structure to escalate into. There is no sponsor, no change window, no incident review board and no TAM, so a procedure built around a governance chain that does not exist stalls the ticket while looking procedurally correct. What they carry over wrongly from SMB is the exact inverse: assuming there is no contract. There is one, it has a number in it, and it will be read aloud during the first bad week — usually by our own account executive, in front of the customer.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | the one admin who owns the tool alongside four other jobs, occasionally a colleague they delegated to, never a support team |
| typical_resolution_hours | 24 |
| volume_shape | moderate volume, moderate complexity, clustered around onboarding, seat and plan changes, integration work and the weeks before renewal |
| staffing_model | pooled generalists with a light second line; a CSM shared across dozens of accounts and no named engineer |
| coverage | business hours in one or two regions; anything wider is an upgrade line item rather than an operational decision |
| automation_level | moderate — this admin will self-serve willingly, but the documentation was written either for developers or for consumers and they are neither |
| buyer | a department head or an operator close to the founders, who picked the support tier as a checkbox late in the cycle |
| typical_cycle_days | 45 |
| typical_acv | five figures, with support bundled into the plan rather than priced separately |
| committee_size | small — one or two people, and one of them is frequently the person now filing the tickets |
| decision_style | pragmatic and fast at purchase, forensic at renewal; the contract goes unread until something goes wrong and is then read very carefully |
| notes | The plan boundary is the daily negotiation surface. Every mid-market support org discovers that a meaningful share of its escalations are not about a defect at all — they are about something the customer believes they bought. Whether that gets handled as a support failure or routed to the account owner is the single highest-leverage routing decision in this branch, and it is made dozens of times a week by whoever happens to pick up.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement`

Requires `plan`, `entitled_channels`, `entitled_first_response_minutes`, `expires_at`, `last_verified_at`


> The entitlement is checkable and nobody checks it, which is a different failure from enterprise (where it is checked and argued over) and from SMB (where there is nothing to check). `last_verified_at` earns its place here specifically: the useful question in this segment is not what the plan says but whether anyone has looked this quarter. The check belongs before the first reply, not before the breach — by breach time the promise has already been made in the customer's head.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.sla_target`

Requires `is_contractual`, `clock_state`


> Half the targets in a mid-market queue are internal service standards and half are contractual, and in the tooling they look identical. Missing an internal one costs goodwill; missing a contractual one costs credits and gets quoted at renewal. Treating them as the same thing produces the characteristic mid-market pattern of over-serving the accounts that cannot invoice us and under-serving the two that can.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.requester`

Requires `is_admin`, `is_named_contact`, `product_familiarity`


> This person is not a requester in the enterprise sense — they are the account. Their product familiarity is the ceiling on how fast anything gets diagnosed, and their departure is an account-level event that should propagate to the renewal risk, not a contact record going stale. An org that models them as one contact among many loses the only early warning this segment reliably emits.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.escalation`

Requires `origin`, `receiving_owner_ref`, `reason`


> `origin` carries more weight here than in any other branch. A mid-market escalation usually enters sideways through our own AE or CSM, and one logged as customer-originated loses the load-bearing fact that a colleague with a quota is now a participant. The receiving owner is frequently a commercial owner rather than a technical one, which is the correct answer and looks wrong on an escalation dashboard built for enterprise.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.churn_risk`


> Renewal is one person's decision, taken partly on how the last bad ticket felt and almost never discussed with us in advance. There is no procurement review to surface it and no QBR in which it becomes visible, so the support record is the leading indicator — specifically the tickets that were resolved correctly and slowly.

## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional**


> Segment branch, and the one most likely to be run by inheritance from the wrong parent. An org that grew up-market brings SMB reflexes and misses the contract; an org that grew down-market brings enterprise procedure and stalls on governance that was never there. Both failures are recorded in the description because both are recoverable once named.
